items.title: 4.1.7.2 Types of Trees (Binary Tree, AVL Trees)

source_refs.note: Topic 4.1.7.2 Types of Trees (PDF 111-112, printed 108-109), as printed: Binary Tree and AVL Trees with Figures 4.9 and 4.10 (4.10 redrawn, Book correction kept).

blocks.text: Trees come in various types, each with its own unique structure and purpose. There are two common types of trees: Binary Trees and AVL Trees. These types help in organizing and managing data in efficient ways.

A binary tree is a hierarchical data structure in which each node can have at most two children, known as the left and right children as shown in Figure 4.9. This structure is analogous to a family tree, where each individual may have up to two descendants, ensuring a well-organized and balanced arrangement of data for efficient management and retrieval.
Example: In the binary tree example shown in figure 4.9:

items: The ”Grandparent" is the root, and it has two children, “Parent1" and ”Parent2”.
Each parent can have their own children (like “Child1”, “Child2”. etc.).

blocks.alt: Binary tree of circles joined by arrows: Grandparent at the top points to Parent2 and Parent1; Parent2 points to Child4 and Child3; Parent1 points to Child2 and Child1.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.9: Binary Tree Representation of a Family Tree (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.9).

blocks.text: An AVL tree is a type of binary tree that keeps itself balanced, meaning the height of the tree is managed carefully. If one side of the tree starts getting too tall compared to the other, the tree rearranges itself to maintain balance.

Example: Imagine you are organizing books on shelves. You want to make sure that the shelves are balanced, so one side isn't heavier than the other. This is similar to an AVL tree as shown in Figure 4.10.

blocks.alt: AVL tree with arrows: 20 at the top; 15 as its left child, with 10 on the left and 18 on the right under it; 30 as the right child of 20.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.10: AVL Tree (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.10, with 15, 10 and 18 on the left and 30 on the right as the text describes).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 4.10 is mirrored, with 30 on the left and 15 on the right (18 left of 15); as the text says, 15 (with 10 on its left and 18 on its right) is on the left of 20 and 30 on the right, as drawn above.

items: The tree stays balanced after each new number (like a book on a shelf) is added.
The height difference between the left side (with nodes 15, 10, 18) and the right side (with node 30) remains minimal, keeping the tree balanced.
